name: 8 - Building a Better Conversation Transcript
content:
**Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** 40 million people, all these different regulations, working across various different levels of government. And so, we'll be talking a little bit about the whiz-bang technology, but for me, the real exciting thing about this is how we managed to do this through, and are continuing to manage to do this through, the state of California, which is a very complex implementation environment that Jeffrey and his team were able to navigate very successfully. So, as most of you know, this is a process that has a variety of different phases. What I want to call out here is that we did two really big engagements related to the LA fire. So it wasn't just a one-and-done. We recruited participants — we can talk more about our methods later — but then we had them come in and essentially tell us what they had on their minds. It was a little bit more structured than that, but we made sure that we weren’t open-washing the process. We weren’t just going to people to have them tell us what we already think; we were going to them in a fairly open-ended way, saying: *What is it that you want to be talking about? What are the things you want to deliberate on, exchange on, provide information to the government on?* And then there was a second phase — and it’s this second phase that the report being released tomorrow covers — where, again, the tech is cool, but the intergovernmental relations work required to make this happen is, to me, the even cooler part. We brought back to them: *Okay, we heard all these different things from you — which of these would you prioritize, and in what way, and what do you want to direct the state, city, or county to do?* And I’ll just say before handing it back to Jeffrey: the use of AI was really interesting. We've all been to stakeholder meetings or public engagements where people submit comments online, and before AI, we really weren’t able to do much with it. Humans are not good at dealing with mountains of qualitative data. And of course, we keep humans in the loop — we double-check everything, we make our own sense of the sense the tools create. But what excites me is that these tools allow us to *listen at scale* . And if you are truly listening, you hear a lot of different things. So, let me hand it over to Jeffrey to talk about what we did and what we heard.
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Thank you, Mike. It has been a very interesting journey in terms of how we’ve been able to bring together the different tools, technology, stakeholders, and relationships through the bureaucracy of the state of California. I’m happy to take questions later. One of the greatest innovations here was simply that we were able to get started on something like this, and we had the full support of the administration. One reason it’s so rare to see something like this sponsored by a government entity is that, in many respects, an elected official must commit to delivering outcomes before those needs have been communicated by the public — a big risk for an elected. This administration was willing to take that risk, and we’re continuing to work on it.
 
 As Micah mentioned, this presentation focuses on the agenda-setting phase. That will be the context for the next few slides. I’ll also talk about Phase 2 engagement and what that report will look like. I saw in the poll that many of you are interested in the technology and how to use these tools, so I’ll cover that too.
 
 It’s probably hard to see, but the goal is simply to give you a look inside the platform. It’s important to recognize that, in addition to using new technology to listen at scale, this is also a design challenge. From ODI’s perspective, when we socialized this idea within the administration and with LA County and LA City officials, people asked: *Isn’t this just more social media? Isn’t this just going to be another toxic stew? We already have Nextdoor, Reddit — why do we need this?* The key takeaway was that this platform is intentionally designed by humans motivated to drive meaningful public engagement and deliberation.
 
 A couple of keys: this is time-boxed. And recruitment is done with purpose — we invite people for a specific conversation. Once they join, we welcome them and set the stage for productive and civil engagement — for example, the Pledge of Civility. It’s simple: users promise to be constructive. It’s remarkable how effective this is. We also had a moderation policy and human moderators. We moderated out very few comments — fewer than 5%, most of which were advertisements for commercial services.
 
 This is part of what the experience looked like for the agenda-setting phase. Again, our goal was to hear from people about their priorities — not presume we already knew. We spoke with community-based organizations and LA officials beforehand to understand the landscape, and from those conversations we created a short list of broad topics. One was debris removal and environmental recovery. We asked: *In your world, how important is this for further deliberation? How much should we focus on this in the next phase?*
 
 We used the Othello platform, which was great for driving conversations. People not only weighed in on importance but engaged with each other. This made it feel participatory — not like comments disappearing into a void.
 
 This screenshot from the agenda-setting report shows priority levels. We found key tensions — one major tension was rebuilding quickly versus rebuilding with lasting resilience. People debated trade-offs: fast-tracking permitting vs. undergrounding power lines, for example.
 
 Participants saw results updated in real time — how they voted, how the community voted, distributions across topics. We indexed toward *consensus* — defined as high support and low opposition — rather than majority rule.
 
 Here are some key stats: over 3,000 affected survivors and residents invited; over 2,500 comments left between March and August; resulting in 19 policy recommendations. We used AI — specifically Claude Sonnet integrated into Snowflake — to analyze comments and convert long narrative responses into policy actions. We then worked with subject-matter experts to narrow those to 19 feasible, community-aligned options.
 
 There were over 1,500 comments and replies — a powerful community conversation. We extracted data into our environment, ran topic modeling, and used GenAI to pull key themes and connect them to verbatim quotes. This combination of abstract themes and real voices was powerful for reporting to the governor’s office.
 
 One striking quote from a follow-up survey: *“I’ve been reaching out to everyone involved in the recovery effort and received not one reply. Not slammed doors — just no one answering my knock.”* Hearing that is moving, and it reinforces why this work matters.
 
 Before handing it back to Beth, I’ll ask Micah if there’s anything I missed.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Wonderful, thank you so much. And let me just say for everybody here: my apologies — the Q&A button has somehow disappeared under many other new Zoom features. If you would just label your messages with the word *“question”* , we will see it. I'll help get us started with a few questions and then turn it over to the group. If people have clarifying questions like the one that was asked in the chat — *“What was the name of the platform?”* — please feel free to type those and we'll answer them there. Micah and Jeffrey also have team members here who can help answer specific details like number of comments, etc.
 
 So let me first ask you: who came to whom, and how did you get to “yes”? Because you were under significant crisis and political pressure. The governor is politically ambitious and under attack; the fires were a sensitive and difficult time. How did you get to yes on this project? And was it the crisis itself that made it possible?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Thank you. A little background: engaged democracy, deliberative democracy as a movement is something Governor Newsom has been interested in for a long time. It was in his book *Citizen Bill* in 2013. Audrey Tang kicked off similar work in Taiwan in 2014. There was momentum, and Governor Newsom was always interested — he experimented a bit with participatory budgeting when he was mayor of San Francisco.
 
 It’s telling that even though he wanted to get something like this off the ground inside the administration earlier, it didn’t come together until ODI had matured a bit — once I’d built out the team with the necessary skill sets. Then we were asked, outside of any crisis, to stand up this program. Our first use case was supposed to focus on the impact of social media on youth, sponsored by the First Partner’s Office and the California Department of Public Health.
 
 As we were preparing, advisors said we needed to talk to Micah and the Carnegie Foundation to connect us with experts. So Amy Tong, then Secretary of the Government Operations Agency and my boss, called Micah. We got to work. I assembled a team at ODI, and we were just about to kick off the first use case when the fires happened. The governor called an all-hands meeting and said this was the number one statewide priority — and also the number one priority for Engaged California.
 
 We heard from many people: *“Don’t do it. Too risky. Too sensitive. People are in trauma. Don’t pilot new tech during this.”* Many urged us not to proceed. But the governor insisted: *“We’re doing it.”*
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Yeah — that was a fun phone call: “Hey Micah, you know that thing we’ve been working on for nine months? We’re now doing something completely different immediately.”
 
 But we had built the groundwork. And I want to emphasize — as a nonpartisan organization — that at no point has this project been political or partisan. That’s unusual, given the context you framed, Beth. But it has been encouraging. This isn’t a partisan point-scoring exercise; it’s complex and hard. You wouldn’t choose this as a political stunt. We’re working on what’s next in democracy, improving it — not partisan messaging.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** It’s a good thing you didn’t do the social media topic, given what has unfolded since — the governor’s Twitter being second funniest only to New Jersey’s. Which brings me to the next question: how did you decide *which* question to ask? There are many ways to ask: *What should we do about the fires? What do you think? What do you feel? What policy should we adopt?* You said you used AI later to extract policy ideas, but how did you pick the initial question? It’s not always easy.
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Micah, do you want to take that? We had an advisory board and program design partners from various institutions who guided this. They were essential to designing the question.
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Absolutely. One of our program design partners, Avre Valentine from the Public Good Group, advised us to ask the most open-ended question possible at that stage. If you want to truly listen at scale and bring people into dialogue, ask something like: *“How have the fires impacted you?”* The initial engagement included a “throat-clearing” prompt: *“Anything you want to tell us?”* before introducing structure. This was important.
 
 **Jeffery Marino** In the second phase, where we had the policy options, we designed options around trade-offs. For example: fast-tracking permitting to develop accessory dwelling units. That brings in tensions around density, NIMBY vs. YIMBY, speed vs. careful rebuilding. Structuring options around real tensions generated rich dialogue that AI tools could then analyze.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** We had a conversation recently with faculty from Stanford and UVA about summarizing citizen comments with AI. One issue was whether it’s easier to extract *opinion* , *know-how* , *sentiment* , etc. Here, it seems you focused on extracting *know-how* — actionable ideas. How did that work? Will you continue doing that? How can these tools help provide good experiences for residents and useful outputs for policymakers?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Great question. Our data team debated this extensively. We started with “How do people feel?” but quickly realized our goal was: *What do people want to happen?* That led us to focus on know-how — the “what” more than the “why.” Sentiment analysis is valuable, especially for showing residents they were heard. But for program goals, we need actionable insights. As the program evolves, we may integrate deeper sentiment analysis alongside policy-oriented outputs.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Carolyn Lukensmeyer noted in the chat — long before Audrey Tang, Carolyn was pioneering deliberative engagement. Others like the Jefferson Center were early leaders. Do you see AI as crucial to *why now* ? Or does it simply allow us to do things qualitatively different than before? What were you able to do now that you couldn’t before?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** We brought in many people with deep experience running in-person deliberative processes. I’ve been part of huge in-person deliberative polling exercises. In those, you get amazing depth — but it’s hard to understand what is actually happening in aggregate. AI lets you focus attention: *What did quieter voices say? What did this demographic emphasize?* With large qualitative datasets and thoughtful humans guiding the process, AI can actually help us listen better than we could in a room where a few voices dominate. That’s part of the “why now.”
 
 **Jeffery Marino** And it helped us in the political environment. There’s pressure to move fast and deliver results. Doing this asynchronously and using AI to turn large amounts of information into actionable insights — without needing huge facilitation resources — helped us succeed and deliver something meaningful.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Let me bring in some chat questions. Richard asked: is this “Claude out-of-the-box”? How sophisticated was the topic modeling? Can others replicate this? Was it good prompting by humans, or more technical?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Good question. Micah’s team and ours are continuing technology discovery. We will publish a white paper mapping the technology landscape. Othello has some analytics built in, but not the GenAI-powered parsing we needed. Since we have data engineers and data scientists, we built a data integration pipeline to extract information into Snowflake. Claude was available natively via Snowflake, which helped — we didn’t need to procure AI, which is still difficult in government. We’re exploring tools that have more of this “out of the box,” requiring less technical lift.
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** We’re looking at Remesh, GoVocal, Polis, Cortico — many tools. But I want to emphasize: you need not just technical expertise, but intergovernmental expertise. Big tech vendors rarely understand state processes. Without that expertise, you risk engaging residents and then producing nothing of substance — which is worse than doing nothing. You need the ability to navigate intergovernmental realities. That’s why ODI is so valuable.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** And you can’t underestimate the importance of having decision-makers at the table. You need someone who can act. Another question: did you encounter negative attitudes toward AI?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Not nearly as much as expected.
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Yes. Given the topic, I expected this to become a complaint box. But people were constructive. And we didn’t lead with AI — it was backend infrastructure. AI is just another tool; if used well, it’s helpful.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Hamburg told us the same — AI is in the background, not foreground. Chris asked about astroturfing. Are you worried about organized lobbying campaigns, bots, etc.? Does this get in the way of scaling?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** We’ve had productive conversations about sustainability and long-term viability. Capture is the biggest risk — capture by executive leadership or by special interests. We are working on a governance model. The program is fragile. We must balance proximity to power (to drive action) with independence. Leadership will change in 14 months. We need strategies to preserve the integrity of the program.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** How do you institutionalize this across agencies? How do you push this out so agencies can run processes themselves?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** One key is sortition. These engagements are carefully designed; they’re not open comment boxes. Random, representative samples help avoid capture. This wasn’t a formal sortition process, but it’s part of future plans.
 
 Also, this technology is valuable across policy phases — especially implementation. Regulatory comment processes are often captured by those being regulated. This helps bring in everyday residents.
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Scaling: ODI could become a center of excellence. Other departments won’t have data scientists, but they *can* run the community engagement, outreach, audience recruitment, and on-the-ground components. We might support the tech; they manage the engagement. This modular approach could scale.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Wonderful. A few announcements before the hour. We have more sessions coming up, we’re experimenting with a virtual wine-and-cheese format. Speakers can stay if they’d like; others may go. We’ll share tomorrow’s report when it’s released. In the last minute: what’s your one line of advice for people who want to do this themselves?
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Start. It’s always the hardest part. We began by putting one foot in front of the other and just didn’t stop.
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** I agree — start.
 
 **Jeffery Marino** Thank you. I need to drop. It was a pleasure talking with you, Beth, and the InnovateUS team. If anyone wants to take a deeper dive, we are open to sharing resources and methods.
 
 **Beth S. Noveck** Thank you, and thanks to everyone for coming. Those who want to stay and chat, please do — we will leave the room open.
 
 **Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS)** We are keeping the session open for questions and comments. Please feel free to turn on your cameras. Let’s continue the conversation. Stefan, please go ahead.
 
 **Stephen Buckley** Thanks. I put a question in the chat about user experience. You said you received good anecdotal feedback. But was there anything more systematic — like a survey — so that others who replicate this can compare apples to apples?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Yes. We ran a follow-up survey with a subset of participants. ODI has excellent UX experts — they designed user-experience surveys and integrated UX into the platform design. But the biggest factor affecting user experience is whether anything actually *happens* as a result. The engagement experience matters, but so do outcomes.
 
 **Stephen Buckley** So it’s both the “afterglow” and whether a “baby was born.” Two different questions.
 
 **Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS)** Thank you. Chris, you’re next.
 
 **Chris Bui – Better Together America** Micah, I’m curious how your experience at California Forward informed this. We always wished we could get the general public engaged, not just those in the room. Do you think the regional sustainability network is a good platform for this?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Absolutely. I recently spoke at the California Economic Summit. Grass-tops organizations aren’t always representative of the broader public. AI-supported sense-making can complement regional convenings and help bring in voices that are missing.
 
 **Chris Bui – Better Together America** Follow-up: how do we get accurate representation? In Emeryville, we used a consistent group of 200 residents. How do you solve for that?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Sortition. We’re planning a civic assembly in Oakland using random, representative selection. This wasn’t part of Engaged California’s first iterations, but it’s essential going forward.
 
 **Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS)** Siseko, please.
 
 **Siseko Siwali** How are you dealing with true data vs. accurate data? True data is lived experience; accurate data is measured or topic-based. They sometimes conflict. In South Africa, we found big differences between daily conversations and structured research interviews. How do you handle that?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** I think I have more to learn from you on this. But it comes back to the questions you ask. Asking complex, technical questions (as we do in California’s ballot measures) yields poor data. Our open-ended questions elicited lived experience — *true* data. People could speak about their actual experience during the crisis. That produced relatively objective and useful input.
 
 **Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS)** Chris, your turn.
 
 **Chris Bui – Better Together America** Many groups want to “fix democracy” but don’t partner with municipalities from the start. They innovate civic engagement in silos. What advice do you have?
 
 **Micah Weinberg – Carnegie Endowment** Happy to meet — we’re both in the Bay Area. But broadly: we must explain how this solves government workers’ real problems. “Democracy isn’t good enough” is not a problem agencies are tasked to solve. They *are* tasked with getting better information for service delivery, regulatory design, etc. You also must legalize new processes — public comment laws often prevent innovation. Working with agencies early matters.
 
 **Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS)** Stephen?
 
 **Stephen Buckley** A follow-up: many groups are trying to save democracy, which is too big. But if you show how this works for everyday issues — like where to put a bike lane — that’s powerful. Simple stories based on real life help.
